subtopics.title: Summit Theme, Principles and Objectives
subtopics.summary: India hosted the India AI Impact Summit 2026 at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, presented as the first multilateral AI summit in the Global South. The summit marked a shift from a Western safety-first model to an impact-first, developmental approach to AI, under the theme 'Sarvajana Hitaya, Sarvajana Sukhaya'. Its work rests on three Sutras and seven Chakras, and it set out four key objectives.
facts: Held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi; described as the 1st multilateral AI summit in the Global South
Signals a shift from a Western safety-first model to an impact-first, developmental AI paradigm
Theme: 'Sarvajana Hitaya, Sarvajana Sukhaya' (Welfare for All, Happiness for All)
3 Sutras: People (Inclusive Development), Planet (Ethical Innovation), Progress (Sustainable Societal Impact)
7 Chakras (Priority Cooperation Areas): Healthcare, Agriculture, Education, Governance, Climate action, Digital Economy, Social Inclusion
Objective 1: translate global AI discussions into development outcomes aligned with IndiaAI Mission and Digital India
Objective 2: promote responsible and ethical AI, addressing algorithmic bias, privacy protection and accountability
Objective 3: build partnerships between governments, startups, academia and industry
Objective 4: position India as a Global AI Hub and promote an indigenous AI ecosystem
Switzerland will host the 2027 World Summit on AI in Geneva

subtopics.title: New Delhi Declaration and Its Seven Pillars
subtopics.summary: The New Delhi Declaration on AI was adopted at the summit and focuses on inclusive, ethical and development-oriented AI. It is endorsed by 87 countries and 2 international organisations and is built around seven pillars supported by voluntary global initiatives. Separately, the New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments form a voluntary framework signed by frontier AI companies and domestic innovators.
facts: Adopted at the India AI Impact Summit 2026; focuses on inclusive, ethical and development-oriented AI
Endorsed by 87 countries and 2 international organisations (European Union and International Fund for Agricultural Development)
Built around 7 pillars, each supported by voluntary global initiatives
Charter for Democratic Diffusion of AI: promotes locally relevant AI ecosystems and Global South participation
Global AI Impact Commons: platform for sharing successful AI solutions and replicating best practices globally
Trusted AI Commons: repository of tools, benchmarks, safety standards and best practices
International Network of AI for Science Institutions: connects research institutions for collaborative scientific innovation
AI for Social Empowerment Platform: platform for sharing scalable AI solutions for social welfare
AI Workforce Development Playbook & Reskilling Principles: guidance for governments to prepare workforce for AI transformation
Guiding Principles on Resilient & Efficient AI: focus on sustainability and energy-efficient AI systems

subtopics.title: M.A.N.A.V. Roadmap and Previous AI Summits
subtopics.summary: The Prime Minister unveiled the human-centric M.A.N.A.V. Framework for Ethical and Inclusive AI at the summit, with each letter standing for one principle. The booklet also traces earlier global AI summits: the UK's 1st AI Safety Summit and its Bletchley Declaration, the Seoul Summit of 2024 and the 3rd AI Action Summit held in Paris in 2025.
facts: Prime Minister unveiled the human-centric M.A.N.A.V. Framework for Ethical and Inclusive AI at the summit
M: Moral and Ethical Systems; AI must be fair and transparent, subject to human oversight
A: Accountable Governance; clear institutional responsibility, transparent regulatory rules, strong oversight
N: National Sovereignty; securing critical datasets, strengthening domestic compute, indigenous model development
A: Accessible and Inclusive AI; democratise benefits, bridge the digital divide, reach marginalised populations
V: Valid and Legitimate Systems; trust, safety and legal compliance, important given deepfakes and misinformation
UK hosted the 1st AI Safety Summit and adopted the Bletchley Declaration on AI's promises and risks
Bletchley Declaration emphasises aligning AI with human intent, safeguarding rights, safety, ethics and accountability
AI Seoul Summit took place in 2024, co-hosted by the Republic of Korea and the UK government
3rd AI Action Summit was held in 2025 in Paris, France

subtopics.title: Sovereign Models and Domain Platforms
subtopics.summary: India's sovereign AI models include Sarvam's large language models, the Vikram chatbot, Gnani.ai's Vachana speech model and BharatGen's Param2 17B. Bharat GenAI develops foundational models tailored to 22 Indian languages, while BODH, SAHI, VoicERA and BHASHINI cover health and language platforms. The Bio-AI Mulankur Hubs link AI with biotechnology under the BioE3 policy.
facts: Sarvam-30B and Sarvam-105B by Sarvam AI are large language models that generate human-like text
Sarvam's Vikram is a multilingual chatbot for seamless conversations across Indian languages
Vachana is a text-to-speech model by Gnani.ai that supports 12 Indian languages
Param2 17B is a multilingual foundational AI model by BharatGen
Bharat GenAI: India's first government-supported initiative for sovereign foundational AI models, spearheaded by IIT Bombay
Bharat GenAI models are tailored to 22 Indian languages and cover text, text-to-speech and vision-language
BODH: privacy-preserving benchmarking platform for health AI using diverse, real-world health data; positioned under Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission
SAHI (Strategy for Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare for India): national framework for responsible AI integration in healthcare
VoicERA: open-source, end-to-end voice AI stack serving as a national execution layer for multilingual voice AI
BHASHINI (Bhasha Interface for India): AI-powered national language translation and speech platform under Digital India

subtopics.title: Flagship Initiatives, Funding and Global Bodies
subtopics.summary: India's flagship initiatives include the IndiaAI Mission, which builds AI infrastructure around sovereign GPUs, and programmes for startups, women and youth. The summit highlighted large pledges, including $20 billion for frontier deep-tech research. Global context comes from GPAI, established in 2020, and the G7 Hiroshima AI Process, which sets guardrails for advanced AI systems.
facts: IndiaAI Mission: builds AI infrastructure with 10,000 GPUs initially, backed by a budget of 10,372 crore
GPU target: initially 10,000, achieved 38,000, with 20,000 new GPUs being added
IndiaAI Mission 2.0 aims to onboard 38,000 sovereign GPUs and advance the National Compute Portal and strategic compute autonomy
AIRAWAT: India's largest AI supercomputing system at C-DAC Pune, manufactured by Netweb Technologies
AIRAWAT stands for AI Research, Analytics and Knowledge Assimilation
AI for ALL: identifies scalable AI solutions for development challenges, implemented with Startup India
AI by HER: promotes women-led AI innovation, implemented with NITI Aayog's Women Entrepreneurship Platform
YUVAi: encourages AI innovation among youth aged 13-21
$20 billion pledged for frontier deep-tech research
GPAI (Global Partnership on AI): established 2020, officially proposed by France and Canada; secretariat in Paris (OECD); 2024 summit held in India

quizzes.passage:
India hosted a major AI gathering in 2026, and the event was presented as a turning point in how the technology is approached. Earlier global discussions on AI were described as following a Western safety-first model, which placed the management of risk ahead of other concerns. The summit signalled a different direction, an impact-first developmental paradigm in which AI is judged by the outcomes it produces for people. Under this approach, attention is directed to priority cooperation areas such as healthcare and agriculture, where AI can be put to practical use.

The gathering was planned around a guiding message of collective welfare and was organised around a set of guiding principles that shape how its work is framed. Its discussions were meant to move beyond broad global conversations and towards practical, scalable applications. Several objectives were set for the event, and these were meant to guide its outcomes. Participants were also expected to consider India's role in the field.

Beyond the summit itself, the event was placed within a longer series of international meetings on AI. Earlier summits had addressed the promises and risks of the technology, and their discussions often returned to questions of human intent, safety and accountability. The India gathering was presented as a continuation of that conversation, with a stronger emphasis on development and on the needs of countries in the Global South.

A major artificial intelligence meeting was held in India in 2026, and its organisers presented it as a new chapter for the field. Earlier discussions were described as following a Western safety-first model. The organisers argued for a different starting point, one in which development is central and AI is judged by how far it improves the lives of ordinary citizens. This framing placed the meeting within a longer series of international AI gatherings that had come before it.

The meeting was built around a short guiding phrase that pointed to the welfare of everyone. A set of guiding principles shaped its agenda, covering inclusive development, ethical innovation and sustainable societal impact. Within this framework, the meeting identified priority areas where cooperation could produce results, including health, farming and education.

The meeting was also meant to promote the responsible development of AI. Beyond the gathering itself, the organisers hoped to link its outcomes with national programmes for digital growth and with a growing domestic technology base. Its discussions were expected to move from broad global conversations towards practical applications that can be scaled across a large country.

Some participants were expected to focus on how India's own research institutions and companies could contribute to this work, and the wider aim was to strengthen an indigenous ecosystem for the technology.

Its principles were arranged so that each letter of the framework's name stands for one idea. The principles were presented together as a single design. The framework reflects concerns that have appeared in earlier international meetings on the subject, where the balance between innovation and safety has been a recurring theme. The framework was unveiled by the Prime Minister during the summit.

Earlier summits form part of the background to this work. A series of such meetings has been held in different countries, and the first of them was focused on risks from advanced systems. Later gatherings followed in other years and places. Taken as a whole, the series of meetings shows how the subject has been discussed over several years.

The principles in the framework touch on several themes, including the need for systems to be fair and transparent, the importance of clear responsibility in governance, and the value of strengthening domestic capacity. They also address the spread of false content online. Taken together, these ideas show how the framework tries to connect technology with public purpose. These themes are presented as part of a human-centric approach.

India's 2026 summit saw the unveiling of a human-centric framework for ethical and inclusive artificial intelligence. The framework is built on a set of principles, each represented by one letter of its name. Its principles address several concerns, including the design of AI systems, the responsibility of institutions, the role of domestic capacity and data, and the role of trust in an era of misinformation.

The framework was introduced against a background of earlier international meetings on AI, held in several countries. The series began with a meeting focused on the risks linked to advanced AI systems. Later summits followed in other years and cities, and the subject has remained on the international agenda.

Each principle in the framework is meant to be read alongside the others, and together they form one human-centric approach. The framework therefore links technical design with questions of governance, legitimacy and public trust. Its ideas were presented as part of a wider effort to make AI serve people.

Several earlier meetings addressed similar questions from different angles, and the summit's framework was placed within that wider international context. The subject has been discussed in forums across different countries, and the India gathering was one more step in that conversation. Its framework formed part of that wider debate.

quizzes.passage:
India's push for sovereign artificial intelligence has produced a range of models and platforms, some built for general language tasks and others for specific sectors. The idea behind sovereign AI is that a country should be able to develop, control and deploy its own AI technologies. Several domestic firms and research bodies are working on such models, and their work has been presented as part of the national effort.

Language is a central concern in this work. Indian languages are numerous, and systems that handle them require careful development. Some of the national efforts focus on translation and speech, so that people can use digital services in their own languages. Others concentrate on text generation, aiming to produce fluent output that reads naturally to users. Such work must also reflect the cultural contexts of different communities.

Health is another major area. Platforms in this field are intended to test AI systems on real-world data while protecting privacy. Some of them are linked to government health missions that aim to help their use spread across the country.

Biotechnology is also part of the picture. Policies that connect AI with life sciences aim to bring computer models and laboratory work closer together. Such efforts are presented as a way to link research with national priorities.

quizzes.passage:
Sovereign artificial intelligence refers to a country's ability to develop, control and deploy its own AI technologies, and India has pursued this goal through a number of models and platforms. Some are designed for language, others for sectors such as health and biotechnology. The work is carried out by private companies, research institutions and public bodies, which together form a national effort.

Indian languages present a particular challenge for developers. The country has many languages, and a model that works well in one may perform less well in another. Some platforms therefore concentrate on speech and translation, helping citizens use digital services in their own language. Other efforts focus on generating written text in a fluent and natural form.

In health, platforms are being built to test AI systems against real-world data while protecting patient privacy. National frameworks also set out how AI may be integrated into healthcare services. Several of these initiatives sit within existing government missions.

Biotechnology forms another part of the picture. Policies that connect AI with the life sciences aim to bring computer models and laboratory work closer together, so that predictions can be checked by experiments. Such efforts are presented as a way to link research with national priorities.
